title: Redwood Dedicated Release Notes (Draft) — Burst Capacity (Beta) — 2025-10
author: Lauren Bishop
body:
h1. Redwood Dedicated — Burst Capacity (Beta) (Target release: 2025-10)

*Document status:* Draft (internal) — customer-facing language, final availability, and pricing subject to change during beta.

h2. Summary
Burst Capacity (Beta) adds a contractable way for *Redwood Dedicated* tenants to temporarily exceed their reserved baseline capacity during short-lived traffic spikes. When enabled, a tenant may be admitted to a controlled shared *burst pool* (per region / GPU type), subject to strict guardrails designed to protect:
* the tenant’s baseline performance, and
* other Dedicated tenants, and
* the core Hosted fleet.

This beta focuses on *strict admission control* (hard limits, saturation gates, cooldowns) rather than preemptive eviction.

h2. What’s included in this beta
* *Burst enablement per Dedicated tenant* (opt-in only).
* *Customer-configurable guardrails* (e.g., max burst concurrency, max burst TPS/token rate, cooldown).
* *Burst-aware routing behavior* (baseline → burst → fallback/deny) with deterministic policy evaluation.
* *Customer-visible transparency* (headers + metrics surfaced in Console) and internal SRE dashboards/alerts.
* *Shadow metering* for burst vs baseline usage attribution (invoicing may remain unchanged during beta; see “Billing & metering”).

h2. Who this beta is for
Burst Capacity is intended for Dedicated customers with:
* predictable or semi-predictable spike events (product launches, weekly batch jobs, marketing campaigns), and
* a desire to avoid permanent over-provisioning while still maintaining strong noisy-neighbor protections.

Burst is *not* intended as a replacement for baseline sizing for sustained step-function growth.

h2. Availability
* *Launch stage:* Private beta (limited design partners)
* *Regions:* Limited to select regions approved per tenant (configured at enablement time)
* *GPU types / pool eligibility:* Limited to burst pools currently provisioned in-region (varies by region)

Your account team will confirm availability for your tenant and target regions.

h2. How Burst Capacity works (customer view)
When Burst is enabled, Redwood attempts to serve requests using the following sequence:
# *Baseline Dedicated capacity* (your reserved pool)
# If baseline is saturated and your burst policy allows it: *Burst pool admission attempt*
# If burst is denied or the burst pool is saturated: *Fallback behavior* (tenant-configured)

h3. Admission control model (high level)
Burst admission is gated by multiple checks, including:
* Tenant burst enablement and pool eligibility
* Per-tenant hard limits (concurrency / token rate)
* Pool saturation gates (protects other workloads)
* Cooldown/backoff after repeated burst denials (prevents thrash)
* Global circuit breaker behavior when a pool is unhealthy

These checks are designed to be *predictable and auditable*.

h2. Customer configuration (opt-in)
Burst Capacity is *not enabled by default*. During beta, enablement is done by Redwood (with customer confirmation) and can be adjusted via agreed-upon policy settings.

h3. Opt-in process
1) *Request enrollment* through your CSM/AE or Support.
   * Provide target region(s), model(s) / endpoints, expected spike shape (duration, peak concurrency/TPS), and acceptable fallback mode.
2) *Redwood provisions/assigns burst pool eligibility* for the tenant.
3) *Redwood applies initial policy defaults* (conservative guardrails).
4) *Customer validates monitoring* (see “Monitoring recommendations”).
5) *Pilot period* with periodic check-ins; Redwood may adjust guardrails based on observed behavior.

h3. Guardrail settings (beta)
Exact field names may vary by tenant integration method during beta. Conceptually, guardrails include:
* *Max burst concurrency* (upper bound for in-flight requests admitted to burst)
* *Max burst token rate / throughput cap* (protects pool and neighbors)
* *Cooldown window* after repeated denials (limits rapid retries)
* *Eligibility constraints* (allowed regions / GPU pool types)
* *Fallback mode* when burst is denied

If you need specific values for a launch event, Redwood recommends setting them at least *5 business days* prior to the event to allow for validation.

h2. Response behavior, errors, and retry guidance
h3. When burst is used
When a request is served from burst capacity, Redwood will surface an indicator to help with forensics and cost/quality analysis.

*Customer-visible indicators (beta):*
* Response headers include a burst indicator and a non-sensitive reason code for routing/admission outcome.
* The Console shows burst vs baseline usage and burst denial rates (availability varies by tenant).

h3. When burst is denied
A burst denial can happen due to tenant limits, pool saturation, cooldown, or pool health protections.

*Expected behavior (beta):*
* If your fallback mode is configured and available, Redwood may route to the configured fallback.
* Otherwise, requests may be rejected with one of the following:
  * *429 Too Many Requests* — policy/limit-driven denial (e.g., tenant burst cap reached, cooldown active)
  * *503 Service Unavailable* — pool health/saturation-driven denial when no safe fallback is available

h3. Retry guidance
* For *429* responses: honor the *Retry-After* header when present. Aggressive immediate retries can extend cooldown and increase denial rates.
* For *503* responses: Redwood recommends exponential backoff with jitter. If the spike is sustained, consider temporarily lowering concurrency or widening acceptable fallback behavior.

If you see unexpected high deny rates during a planned event, contact Support and include request IDs and timestamps.

h2. Monitoring recommendations (customer)
During beta, Redwood strongly recommends customers monitor burst behavior as a first-class capacity signal.

h3. Key metrics to watch
* *Burst admission success rate* (admitted / attempted)
* *Burst denial rate* (by reason code when available)
* *Baseline utilization* (are you consistently at baseline cap?)
* *End-to-end latency* (p50/p95/p99), especially during burst usage
* *Error rates* (429/503) and retry volume

h3. Recommended dashboards / views
In Redwood Console (where enabled), monitor:
* Burst usage vs baseline usage over time
* Burst admits/denies and top deny reasons
* Tail latency during burst windows

If you run your own observability stack, Redwood recommends annotating:
* deployment events (config changes), and
* scheduled spike events,
so burst behavior can be correlated with latency and error changes.

h3. Suggested alert thresholds (starting point)
These are starting points; Redwood will tune per workload during beta.
* *Burst deny rate > 5% for 10 minutes* during a planned event
* *p99 latency drift > 20%* compared to baseline week-over-week for the same endpoint
* *429 rate sustained > 1%* on critical endpoints (indicates policy caps or cooldown effects)

h2. Known limitations (beta)
* *No spot-market bursting:* Burst pools are controlled shared pools, not dynamic spot arbitrage.
* *Region constraints:* Burst capacity is not guaranteed in every region; cross-region bursting is not supported unless explicitly configured as a fallback.
* *Best-effort burst availability:* Burst does not change your baseline Dedicated guarantees. Burst admission depends on pool health and saturation gates.
* *No preemptive eviction guarantees:* v1 prioritizes strict admission control over preemption.
* *Shadow metering:* Burst usage is attributed for analysis and reconciliation, but invoices may not reflect burst charges during early beta.
* *Model and feature compatibility:* Some models/endpoints may not be eligible for burst depending on runtime constraints and pool provisioning.

h2. Billing & metering (beta)
* Redwood will *attribute* usage to *baseline vs burst* in internal metering.
* During beta, *invoicing may remain unchanged* (shadow billing), while Redwood shares periodic reconciliation reports with pilot customers.
* Pricing/packaging terms for GA are not finalized; beta participants will receive written terms specific to their pilot.

h2. Operational notes
* Burst is protected by automated circuit breakers. In rare cases, Redwood may temporarily disable burst for a tenant or region to preserve overall reliability.
* Configuration changes are audit logged. Customers should coordinate planned spikes and any guardrail changes with Redwood to reduce operational risk.

h2. Getting access / support
* To request beta access: contact your CSM/AE or open a Support ticket and mention *“Dedicated Burst Capacity Beta”*.
* When reporting an issue, include:
  * Tenant name / Dedicated deployment ID
  * Region(s)
  * Affected endpoint(s)
  * Approximate timestamps and request IDs
  * Observed 429/503 rates and latency changes

h2. Change log (draft)
* 2025-09-12 — Initial draft created (Lauren Bishop)
* 2025-09-19 — Added customer monitoring recommendations and retry guidance
* 2025-09-25 — Updated error semantics (429 vs 503) and clarified beta limitations
